```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")

# install any missing packages once
pkgs <- c("dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "scales", "knitr", "WDI",
          "countrycode", "mgcv", "randomForest")
new_pkgs <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
if (length(new_pkgs) > 0) install.packages(new_pkgs)

library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(scales)
library(WDI); library(countrycode); library(mgcv); library(randomForest)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
teal <- "#2A8C82"; orange <- "#E8590C"; blue <- "#364FC7"
```

# 1. Introduction and Problem Statement

Tourism supports economic development, employment and cultural exchange, and
governments and businesses plan transport, hotels and marketing around the
number of visitors they expect. Arrivals move with economic conditions, travel
costs and global events such as the 2020 pandemic. This project analyses World
Bank data on international tourist arrivals to answer practical questions: which
countries receive the most visitors, how arrivals have grown, how strongly the
pandemic reduced them, and whether future arrivals can be predicted from past
arrivals.

**Problem statement:** How can historical international tourist arrival data be
analysed to identify tourism trends and predict future arrivals?

# 2. Objectives

1. Import and clean the raw data (missing values, duplicates, regional totals,
   invalid values) and document every change.
2. Identify the largest destinations and how concentrated tourism is.
3. Measure growth and compare trends across selected countries.
4. Quantify the effect of the 2020 pandemic (paired t-test).
5. Measure the relationship between last year's and this year's arrivals
   (Pearson correlation).
6. Predict arrivals with linear regression, a generalized additive model (GAM)
   and a random forest, and compare them using MAE, RMSE and R-squared.

# 3. Dataset

* **Source:** World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI)
* **Indicator:** International tourism, number of arrivals (`ST.INT.ARVL`)
* **Access:** downloaded in R with the `WDI` package for all countries and
  regions, 1960 to 2023, then saved as `tourism_arrivals_raw.csv`
* **Dataset URL:** https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/ST.INT.ARVL
* **Project repository:** *(paste your GitHub link here)*

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| country | Country or region name |
| iso2c, iso3c | Two- and three-letter country codes |
| year | Calendar year |
| arrivals | Number of international tourist arrivals |

```{r load}
data_file <- "tourism_arrivals_raw.csv"

if (file.exists(data_file)) {
  # na.strings = "" keeps Namibia's country code "NA" as text, not missing
  raw <- read.csv(data_file, na.strings = "", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
} else {
  raw <- WDI(country = "all", indicator = c(arrivals = "ST.INT.ARVL"),
             start = 1960, end = 2023)
  write.csv(raw, data_file, row.names = FALSE, na = "")
}

cat("Rows:", nrow(raw), " Columns:", ncol(raw), "\n")
head(raw)
colSums(is.na(raw))
```

The original download has **`r format(nrow(raw), big.mark = ",")` rows and
`r ncol(raw)` columns**. Many country-year combinations have no value, so a
large share of the `arrivals` column is missing.

# 4. Data Preparation

```{r clean}
n_raw     <- nrow(raw)
n_missing <- sum(is.na(raw$arrivals))

tour  <- distinct(raw)                               # duplicates
n_dup <- n_raw - nrow(tour)

tour <- tour %>% filter(!is.na(arrivals))            # missing arrivals

# regional totals (World, regions, income groups) have no continent
tour$cont <- suppressWarnings(countrycode(tour$iso2c, "iso2c", "continent"))
n_agg_entities <- n_distinct(tour$country[is.na(tour$cont)])
n_agg_rows     <- sum(is.na(tour$cont))
tour <- tour %>% filter(!is.na(cont))

n_invalid <- sum(tour$arrivals <= 0)                 # zero or negative values
tour <- tour %>%
  filter(arrivals > 0) %>%
  transmute(country, year = as.integer(year), arrivals = as.numeric(arrivals)) %>%
  arrange(country, year)

n_countries <- n_distinct(tour$country)
```

**Result:** `r n_dup` duplicate rows were removed and `r format(n_missing, big.mark = ",")`
rows with missing arrivals were dropped. `r n_agg_entities` regional totals and
unmatched codes (such as World and income groups, `r n_agg_rows` rows) were
removed so that only countries are compared, and `r n_invalid` rows had zero or
negative arrivals. The clean dataset has **`r format(nrow(tour), big.mark = ",")`**
rows for **`r n_countries`** countries, covering **`r min(tour$year)` to
`r max(tour$year)`**. No values are available after `r max(tour$year)`.

### Modelling data

For modelling we use the log of arrivals and last year's log arrivals (a lag).
The lag is only used when the previous year exists for that country. Years up to
2019 are kept, because the 2020 pandemic is an exceptional shock that last
year's arrivals cannot predict.

```{r model-data}
model_df <- tour %>%
  filter(year <= 2019) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  mutate(log_arr  = log(arrivals),
         log_lag1 = if_else(year - lag(year) == 1, lag(log_arr), NA_real_)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(log_lag1))

dim(model_df)
```

# 5. Analysis

## 5.1 Descriptive statistics (2019)

```{r desc}
d19 <- tour %>% filter(year == 2019) %>% mutate(m = arrivals / 1e6)

desc <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Countries with 2019 data", "Mean (millions)", "Median (millions)",
                "Std. deviation (millions)", "Maximum (millions)"),
  Value = round(c(nrow(d19), mean(d19$m), median(d19$m), sd(d19$m), max(d19$m)), 2))
knitr::kable(desc)
```

The mean is much larger than the median, so a few countries receive very large
numbers of visitors while most receive far fewer.

## 5.2 Largest destinations

```{r top10}
top10 <- d19 %>%
  slice_max(arrivals, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(share = round(100 * arrivals / sum(d19$arrivals), 1))

knitr::kable(top10 %>%
  transmute(Country = country, `Arrivals (millions)` = round(m, 1),
            `Share of all arrivals (%)` = share))

top5       <- d19 %>% slice_max(arrivals, n = 5) %>% pull(country)
top5_share <- round(100 * sum(d19$arrivals[d19$country %in% top5]) /
                      sum(d19$arrivals), 1)
```

The five largest destinations (`r paste(top5, collapse = ", ")`) account for
**`r top5_share`%** of all 2019 arrivals across the `r nrow(d19)` countries with data.

## 5.3 Growth and trends

We compare the five largest destinations plus India.

```{r growth}
selected <- union(top5, "India")
sel <- tour %>% filter(country %in% selected) %>% mutate(arrivals_m = arrivals / 1e6)

growth_tab <- sel %>%
  filter(year <= 2019) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  summarise(first_year = first(year), last_year = last(year),
            first_m = round(first(arrivals) / 1e6, 2),
            last_m  = round(last(arrivals) / 1e6, 2),
            times   = round(last(arrivals) / first(arrivals), 2),
            cagr_pct = round(((last(arrivals) / first(arrivals))^
                                (1 / (last(year) - first(year))) - 1) * 100, 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(cagr_pct))
knitr::kable(growth_tab,
  col.names = c("Country", "First year", "Last year", "First (M)", "Last (M)",
                "Times larger", "Growth per year (%)"))

yoy_df <- sel %>%
  group_by(country) %>% arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(yoy = if_else(year - lag(year) == 1,
                       (arrivals / lag(arrivals) - 1) * 100, NA_real_)) %>%
  ungroup() %>% filter(!is.na(yoy))

yoy_tab <- yoy_df %>%
  filter(year != 2020) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(median_yoy = round(median(yoy), 1),
            lowest = round(min(yoy), 1), highest = round(max(yoy), 1))
knitr::kable(yoy_tab, col.names = c("Country", "Median yearly growth (%)",
                                    "Lowest (%)", "Highest (%)"))
```

Growth is only calculated where the previous year is available. Extreme values,
such as India in 2014 and the United States in 2006, look like changes in how
arrivals are counted and not real growth.

## 5.4 Effect of the pandemic

```{r pandemic}
pan_all <- tour %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2019, 2020)) %>%
  select(country, year, arrivals) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = arrivals, names_prefix = "y") %>%
  filter(!is.na(y2019), !is.na(y2020)) %>%
  mutate(change_pct = (y2020 / y2019 - 1) * 100)

n_pan   <- nrow(pan_all)
med_fall <- round(median(pan_all$change_pct), 1)

pan_sel <- sel %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2019, 2020)) %>%
  select(country, year, arrivals) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = arrivals, names_prefix = "y") %>%
  mutate(change_pct = round((y2020 / y2019 - 1) * 100, 1))
knitr::kable(pan_sel, col.names = c("Country", "2019", "2020", "Change (%)"))
```

Across the `r n_pan` countries with both years, the median change from 2019 to
2020 was **`r med_fall`%**. A missing 2020 value (NA in the table) means the
World Bank has not reported it.

## 5.5 Correlation analysis

```{r corr}
cor_lag <- cor(model_df$log_lag1, model_df$log_arr)
cor.test(model_df$log_lag1, model_df$log_arr)
```

The Pearson correlation between last year's and this year's log arrivals is
**r = `r round(cor_lag, 3)`**, a very strong positive relationship. A country's
arrivals one year are very close to its arrivals the year before.

## 5.6 Hypothesis test: 2019 vs 2020

H0: the mean log arrivals in 2020 equals the mean log arrivals in 2019 (paired
by country). H1: they differ.

```{r ttest}
t_pan <- t.test(log(pan_all$y2020), log(pan_all$y2019), paired = TRUE)
t_pan
avg_change <- round((exp(unname(t_pan$estimate)) - 1) * 100, 1)
```

The paired t-test gives p = `r signif(t_pan$p.value, 3)`. The average country
lost about **`r abs(avg_change)`%** of its arrivals, so we reject H0: arrivals in
2020 were significantly lower than in 2019.

## 5.7 Prediction models

We predict a country's log arrivals from last year's log arrivals and the year
with three models from the course:

* **Linear regression:** a simple, interpretable baseline.
* **GAM (generalized additive model):** learns smooth, non-linear patterns.
* **Random forest (bagging of many trees):** captures complex relationships, but
  cannot predict beyond the range of values it was trained on.

The data is split by time, not at random: training uses 1995 to 2014 and testing
uses 2015 to 2019. Country is not used as a predictor because `randomForest`
cannot handle a factor with more than 53 levels.

```{r models}
train <- model_df %>% filter(year <= 2014)
test  <- model_df %>% filter(year >= 2015)
cat("Train rows:", nrow(train), "| Test rows:", nrow(test), "\n")

set.seed(123)
m_lm  <- lm(log_arr ~ log_lag1 + year, data = train)
m_gam <- gam(log_arr ~ s(log_lag1) + s(year), data = train)
m_rf  <- randomForest(log_arr ~ log_lag1 + year, data = train, ntree = 500)

knitr::kable(round(summary(m_lm)$coefficients, 4), caption = "Linear regression")
knitr::kable(round(summary(m_gam)$s.table, 3), caption = "GAM smooth terms")
knitr::kable(round(importance(m_rf), 1), caption = "Random forest importance")
```

```{r predict}
results <- test %>%
  mutate(pred_lm   = exp(predict(m_lm,  newdata = test)),
         pred_gam  = exp(as.numeric(predict(m_gam, newdata = test))),
         pred_rf   = exp(predict(m_rf,  newdata = test)),
         pred_last = exp(log_lag1))       # benchmark: repeat last year's value

metrics <- function(actual, pred) {
  data.frame(MAE  = mean(abs(actual - pred)),
             RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2)),
             R2   = 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2))
}

a <- results$arrivals / 1e6
metrics_tbl <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "Linear regression", metrics(a, results$pred_lm  / 1e6)),
  cbind(Model = "GAM",               metrics(a, results$pred_gam / 1e6)),
  cbind(Model = "Random forest",     metrics(a, results$pred_rf  / 1e6)),
  cbind(Model = "Repeat last year",  metrics(a, results$pred_last / 1e6)))

knitr::kable(metrics_tbl, digits = 3,
             caption = "Test-set metrics, 2015 to 2019 (MAE and RMSE in millions)")

three      <- metrics_tbl %>% filter(Model != "Repeat last year")
best_model <- three$Model[which.min(three$RMSE)]
best_row   <- metrics_tbl %>% filter(Model == best_model)
base_row   <- metrics_tbl %>% filter(Model == "Repeat last year")
beats_base <- best_row$RMSE < base_row$RMSE
```

**Result:** **`r best_model`** had the lowest RMSE (`r round(best_row$RMSE, 2)`
million), with MAE `r round(best_row$MAE, 2)` million and R-squared
`r round(best_row$R2, 3)`. In the linear model, last year's log arrivals has a
coefficient of `r round(coef(m_lm)["log_lag1"], 3)` and the year term has
p = `r round(summary(m_lm)$coefficients["year", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3)`, so the year adds
little once last year's arrivals is known. The simple benchmark of repeating last
year's value has an RMSE of `r round(base_row$RMSE, 2)` million, so the best model
**`r ifelse(beats_base, "improves on", "does not improve on")`** it.

# 6. Visualization

```{r fig-top10}
ggplot(top10, aes(reorder(country, m), m)) +
  geom_col(fill = teal) + coord_flip() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(m, 1)), hjust = -0.2) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Countries by Tourist Arrivals, 2019",
       x = NULL, y = "Arrivals (millions)") +
  expand_limits(y = max(top10$m) * 1.12)
```

A handful of countries receive far more visitors than the rest, so tourism is highly concentrated.

```{r fig-trend}
ggplot(sel, aes(year, arrivals_m, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "International Tourist Arrivals, Selected Countries",
       x = "Year", y = "Arrivals (millions)", colour = "Country")
```

Most countries grow until 2019 and then fall sharply in 2020. The points show where
data exists, so gaps (for example France, 1998 to 2003) are visible. The jump for
the United States in 2006 looks like a counting change.

```{r fig-log}
ggplot(sel, aes(year, arrivals_m, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_log10() + scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "International Tourist Arrivals (log scale)",
       subtitle = "Equal slopes mean equal percentage growth",
       x = "Year", y = "Arrivals (millions, log scale)", colour = "Country")
```

On a log scale, small and large countries can be compared fairly. India rises
steeply, including a step around 2014, although its absolute arrivals stay small.

```{r fig-growth}
ggplot(yoy_df, aes(year, yoy)) +
  geom_col(fill = teal) +
  facet_wrap(~ country, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Year-on-Year Growth in Arrivals",
       subtitle = "Each panel has its own vertical scale",
       x = "Year", y = "Growth (%)")
```

In normal years growth is small, a few percent. Spikes for India (2014) and the
United States (2006) look like data breaks, and every country falls sharply in 2020.

```{r fig-index}
sel %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  filter(any(year == 1995)) %>%
  mutate(index = arrivals / arrivals[year == 1995] * 100) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, index, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Arrivals Indexed to 1995 = 100",
       x = "Year", y = "Index (1995 = 100)", colour = "Country")
```

Indexing compares each country with its own 1995 level. India reaches about eight
times its 1995 level, helped by the 2014 jump. France is missing because it has no
value for 1995.

```{r fig-pandemic}
sel %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2019, 2020)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(country, arrivals_m, fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("2019" = blue, "2020" = orange)) +
  labs(title = "Arrivals Before and During the Pandemic",
       x = NULL, y = "Arrivals (millions)", fill = "Year") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

ggplot(pan_all, aes(change_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = orange, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(pan_all$change_pct), colour = "red",
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Change in Arrivals from 2019 to 2020, All Countries",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line = median",
       x = "Change (%)", y = "Number of countries")
```

Almost every country lost visitors in 2020. India has no 2020 value in the data, so
it has no bar.

```{r fig-corr}
ggplot(model_df, aes(log_lag1, log_arr)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(title = "Last Year's vs This Year's Arrivals (log scale)",
       subtitle = paste("Pearson r =", round(cor_lag, 3)),
       x = "Log arrivals, previous year", y = "Log arrivals, current year")
```

The points lie almost on a straight line, so arrivals in one year are very close to
arrivals the year before.

```{r fig-pred}
results %>%
  select(arrivals, `Linear regression` = pred_lm, GAM = pred_gam,
         `Random forest` = pred_rf) %>%
  pivot_longer(-arrivals, names_to = "Model", values_to = "predicted") %>%
  ggplot(aes(arrivals / 1e6, predicted / 1e6)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "red") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ Model) +
  labs(title = "Actual vs Predicted Arrivals, 2015-2019",
       x = "Actual (millions, log scale)", y = "Predicted (millions, log scale)")

ggplot(metrics_tbl, aes(reorder(Model, -RMSE), RMSE)) +
  geom_col(fill = teal) + coord_flip() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(RMSE, 2)), hjust = -0.2) +
  labs(title = "Test RMSE by Model (lower is better)",
       x = NULL, y = "RMSE (millions of tourists)") +
  expand_limits(y = max(metrics_tbl$RMSE) * 1.12)
```

Points near the red line are accurate predictions. The random forest flattens at the
largest values and overpredicts the smallest countries, because tree models cannot
predict outside the range they were trained on.

# 7. Results

| Question | Result |
|---|---|
| Largest destination, 2019 | `r top10$country[1]`: `r round(top10$m[1], 1)` million arrivals |
| Concentration | Top 5 countries = `r top5_share`% of arrivals across `r nrow(d19)` countries |
| Fastest growth per year, 1995 to 2019 (selected) | `r growth_tab$country[1]`: `r growth_tab$cagr_pct[1]`% a year (affected by data breaks) |
| Typical yearly growth in normal years | Median `r round(median(yoy_tab$median_yoy), 1)`% across the selected countries |
| Pandemic effect, 2019 to 2020 | Median change `r med_fall`% across `r n_pan` countries |
| Paired t-test, 2019 vs 2020 | Average fall about `r abs(avg_change)`%, p = `r signif(t_pan$p.value, 3)` |
| Last year's vs this year's arrivals | Pearson r = `r round(cor_lag, 3)` |
| Best prediction model | `r best_model`: RMSE `r round(best_row$RMSE, 2)` million, R-squared `r round(best_row$R2, 3)` |
| Beats "repeat last year"? | `r ifelse(beats_base, "Yes", "No")` (benchmark RMSE `r round(base_row$RMSE, 2)` million) |

# 8. Conclusion

Tourism is highly concentrated: `r paste(top5, collapse = ", ")` receive
`r top5_share`% of all arrivals, while India's arrivals are small in absolute
terms. Most selected countries grew steadily until 2019, with yearly growth usually
a few percent. India grew fastest relative to its own 1995 level, but part of this
comes from a jump around 2014 that looks like a change in counting, and the United
States shows a similar jump in 2006. The 2020 pandemic caused a large and
statistically significant fall in arrivals, with a median change of
`r med_fall`% across `r n_pan` countries.

Last year's arrivals explains almost everything in the models (r = `r round(cor_lag, 3)`),
so tourist arrivals in one year are roughly last year's arrivals multiplied by a
growth factor. **`r best_model`** gave the most accurate predictions on the test
years, and the random forest was weakest because it cannot predict values beyond the
range seen in training. A more complex model was not necessarily better here.

Recommended actions: use last year's arrivals as the starting point for short-term
demand planning; keep a margin for shocks like the pandemic, which no model based on
past arrivals can foresee; and check how arrivals are counted before comparing
countries or drawing conclusions from sudden jumps.

**Limitations:** the models predict one year ahead using the actual previous year,
which is easier than forecasting several years ahead; some series have missing years
and breaks, and countries may count arrivals differently; R-squared is dominated by
the largest countries; the data is annual, so seasonality cannot be studied; the
pandemic years are excluded from the models; and the data ends in
`r max(tour$year)`.

**Future scope:** add predictors such as GDP, exchange rates and tourism receipts,
model the pandemic and recovery separately, forecast several years ahead, add monthly
data, and build an interactive dashboard.
